purpose: Monthly research-to-practice watch for CBT Cards. It records new evidence and intervention signals without automatically publishing them as reviewed CBT Cards practices.
publication_boundary: Inclusion in this watch is not clinical validation, treatment advice, or publication in the reviewed /practice/ layer. Candidate wording is original CBT Cards editorial prototyping and is not the studied intervention unless explicitly stated.

cadence.coverage_rule: Review the previous calendar month. Record both first-online and issue-publication dates. An item can enter on either date, but the freshness basis must be explicit and DOI/PMID must be deduplicated across future editions.

editions.label: August 2026
editions.selection_note: Selected high-signal peer-reviewed studies relevant to CBT/ACT mechanisms, brief interventions, just-in-time support, behavioral activation, delivery models, or digital-practice design. This is a curated watch, not a claim of an exhaustive systematic search.
highlights: Imagery-enhanced activity scheduling is the clearest candidate mechanism for a future CBT Cards micro-practice, but the trial used a four-session depression intervention and a wait-list control.
Single-session CBT and ACT both reduced short-term procrastination in students; intervention details are not sufficiently exposed in the abstract to create a faithful practice card yet.

A micro-randomized just-in-time study suggests that gratitude, savoring, and acceptance may have different short-term fit depending on the moment; this is a routing signal, not proof of a universal sequence.
A large behavioral-activation meta-analysis strengthens the evidence context for existing activity-planning content rather than requiring a new practice.
An online group Unified Protocol pilot is a delivery-model signal, not a self-help card.
Adding an app to homework after one-session treatment for childhood phobias did not improve outcomes or at-home practice, a useful negative product-design signal.

items.title: Imagery-enhanced behavioral activation (WIMBA)
items.sample: 168 adults in Germany meeting criteria for a major depressive episode
items.studied_format: Four brief unguided online sessions with psychoeducation, imagery-enhanced activity scheduling, and personalized feedback versus wait-list.
items.finding: Behavioral activation increased more in WIMBA from session 3 through follow-up, and depressive symptoms decreased more than wait-list. The authors call for further trials including an active control.

candidate.prompt: Before a safe planned activity, picture yourself doing it for about 30 seconds. Notice one concrete sensory detail and one realistically rewarding part, then take the smallest start step.
candidate.micro_action: Choose one already-planned safe activity, imagine one rewarding detail briefly, then begin for two minutes.
candidate.boundary: Do not present this as a depression treatment or as the WIMBA protocol. Do not use imagery to override real danger, professional instructions, or required safety steps.

limitations: Clinical depression sample; general-wellness use is an extrapolation.
The CBT Cards prototype is not the tested four-session WIMBA intervention.

items.title: Single-session CBT and ACT for procrastination (CONCRAS)
items.sample: 151 students with recurrent procrastination and a currently postponed task
items.studied_format: Approximately 60-minute face-to-face CBT or ACT single-session intervention versus no-intervention control, with 2-week follow-up.
items.finding: Both CBT and ACT single-session interventions reduced state procrastination more than control, with no significant difference between CBT and ACT. Similar short-term patterns appeared for task anxiety/doubt and several secondary outcomes.
limitations: The abstract does not expose enough intervention procedure detail to derive a faithful CBT Cards micro-practice without inventing content.

items.title: Just-in-time ecological momentary interventions (ALERT)
items.sample: 72 people at increased risk for mental disorders
items.studied_format: 16 days with four daily assessments; two assessments per day were followed by randomized momentary interventions based on gratitude, savoring, cognitive restructuring, or acceptance.
items.finding: Thirty minutes later, gratitude, savoring, and acceptance improved positive affect; gratitude and savoring reduced negative affect; acceptance reduced negative affect particularly during higher-distress moments. Cognitive reappraisal did not improve affect in this trial.

candidate.working_title: Match the Micro-Practice to the Moment
candidate.prompt: If the moment is safe and you want to amplify something already okay, try a brief savoring or gratitude cue. If distress is high, try making room for the feeling before choosing the next safe action.
candidate.micro_action: Choose one context-matched 30–60 second cue instead of opening a long menu of techniques.
candidate.boundary: This is a routing prototype, not an individualized treatment rule. High distress can also signal genuine danger or need for qualified support; do not use acceptance to delay urgent action.

limitations: Small sample and short intervention period.
No inactive control for distal pre/post changes, so longer-term changes cannot be attributed cleanly to the momentary interventions.
One null result for cognitive reappraisal does not establish that cognitive restructuring is generally ineffective.

items.title: Behavioral activation for depression: comprehensive meta-analysis
items.evidence_type: systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
items.studied_format: Behavioral activation across age groups, settings, and comparators.
items.finding: For adult outpatients, behavioral activation outperformed control conditions on average, with substantial heterogeneity; it did not significantly differ from other therapies. Self-guided behavioral activation showed a smaller but significant average effect.
limitations: High heterogeneity for adult outpatient comparisons.
Too few trials for strong estimates in children/adolescents or versus pharmacotherapy.
This updates mechanism-level evidence; it does not validate any exact CBT Cards card or worksheet.

items.title: Online group Unified Protocol pilot in Argentina
items.sample: 39 adults in Argentina with various emotional disorders
items.studied_format: Ten 90-minute online group Unified Protocol sessions versus wait-list.
items.finding: The intervention group improved across the reported post-treatment outcomes versus wait-list, with high satisfaction and perceived usefulness.
limitations: Clinical transdiagnostic group treatment, not a self-guided micro-practice.
Wait-list comparison and one national/cultural context.

items.title: App-supported homework after one-session treatment for childhood phobias
items.journal: Journal of the American Academy of Child & Adolescent Psychiatry
items.studied_format: Standard one-session treatment followed by therapist-provided homework versus an app-supported homework program.
items.finding: Both groups improved, but the app-supported homework program did not improve outcomes or at-home practice; families reported higher satisfaction with the app condition.
limitations: Child clinical phobia treatment context; not directly generalizable to CBT Cards users.
The result tests one specific app-supported homework implementation, not apps in general.
